content.title: Response (1/1)
content.comment:
> The authors investigate how biological brains could achieve disentangled representations. Through a combination of theory and modeling, they provide ample evidence for two key constraints: (1) nonnegative activities and (2) a constraint on energy expenditure in model/real neurons. The work is exceptionally well explained and builds out from these simple principles to explain results in modeling complex artificial data and rodent experiments.

Many thanks!

> Great introduction. Love how the authors presented and explained the proof relating non-neg and efficiency to independent task factors. The related work brings together the parallel investigations of disentangled factors and the use of nonnegativity to do so (e.g., Lee & Seung, 2000) in Neuroscience and ML. Honestly I could go on and on, but this is a brilliant paper. I love how it begins with a simple concept, explains it like I'm five, and then shows that the theory holds in complex situations that are relevant to the large-scale ML and Neuro pursuits of today.

Many thanks!

> Can you add a github link with your code?

We have now included the code as Supplementary Material in this submission.

> Make the text bigger in your figures? It's a little hard to make out. That's it.

We have now increased the size of the text in the figures.

> Are the colored circles in Figure 2 cartoons or real data?

Good spot! They are cartoons - we have now amended the text in the caption.

> In Fig 2, if I'm understanding this correctly, relu and a non-neg activity constraint yield the same performance. 

As shown in the figure, they both disentangle approximately the same amount. If however by performance you mean how well they fit the data, then they both match the data virtually exactly, however the ReLu is ever so slightly worse (r^2 0.99995 vs 0.99998, figure not shown here).

> Does the regularization also affect the signs of the model weights? There's no constraint for non-negative weights, right? Just non-negative activities?

The regularisation does not constrain the sign of the weights. We just used l2 regularisation. Weights in neuroscience can have both excitatory and inhibitory effects, and so we have not tried constraining the sign of model weights. We have, however, tried sparsity on the weights but we did not observe any disentanglement (new appendix A.6 figure).

> What’s the explanation for neurons that show mixed selectivity? Is that just a relaxation on the energy constraint?

That’s a really good question. While we definitely do not yet understand all possible reasons for mixed-selectivity, we can name a few. First, when the factors need to be combined nonlinearly, then mixed selectivity is unavoidable. This is necessary all over the brain as the compositions in our world are not always linear. Second, since our theory is one of optimality, mixed selectivity will occur in the learning process towards this optimum. Third, while theory is about composing factors, this is not always the best way to understand situations, and indeed can only understand situations that are composed of those factors. Other general methods such as kernel regression may be more appropriate in those situations, in which mixed selectivity is prominent. We hope the sections ‘When to disentangle?’ and ‘Mixed-selective cells in the brain’ from the Discussion help here. We are happy to amend it if it is not clear.

> Beautifully presented paper with adroit insights and contributions to ML and Neuro. The work appears reproducible but there's no code release.

Many thanks! Code now provided!

content.title: Response (2/2)
content.comment:
> Is the rodent navigation dataset a new dataset used in this paper? What are the modalities of the given data (measurements)?

This is an artificial dataset that we have generated ourselves. We have clarified this, and described the dataset in additional detail, in appendix A.9. The relevant additional sentences are shown here

*We generate many 16x16 worlds (so 256 locations; nl = 256) where objects can be at random locations. The number of objects in each world is chosen uniformly between 0 and 8. In practice it is not always possible to place every object as we do not permit objects to be closer than 8 units away.*

*From each world we have the following data: {x, o(x), a(x)} for all 256 locations x, where x is a one-hot identifier of location, o(x) is a binary variable of whether there is an object or not at location x, and a(x) is a 4-dimensional vector describing the optimal action - a one or zero in each entry corresponding to North/South/East/West (more than one action could be optimal at each location). Optimal actions are towards the closest object.* 

*We train on this data, with a batch size of 8, i.e. presenting 8 such worlds simultaneously. Each world in the batch is randomly sampled from the above process.*

> Can you elaborate more on your findings in Figure 7? How should one compare the results in Figures 6 and 7?

Figure 7A shows the same results as Figure 6, i.e. for a model trained on a setting where objects move between tasks, however figure 7B shows representations from a model trained on a single task where the objects are in fixed locations. The key difference is that in the 1st case objects move and so their locations are factored from spatial locations, whereas in the 2nd case objects locations are fixed and so entangled with spatial locations. The representations are qualitatively different too. In 7A you get two types of cells - grid cells that are object independent and object dependent cells that are active around objects (like OVCs). Whereas in 7B all cells look similar - they are grid-like but warp their firing fields around objects. Figure 7C quantifies this warping across many different model initialisations - only the entangled task shows this warping. We hope that this clears up the confusion. We currently keep the text as is, though on your further suggestion, we are happy to change text in the paper to help clarify things.

> How would this model perform when K is not matched with the true number of factors? In the case of cell type, how can one interpret the results in terms of the function of each neuron?

K does not need to be matched with the true number of factors. For example there are only two factors in the cell-type experiments, but we use 100 neurons. Similarly, in the unsupervised tasks, the latent layer had 10 neurons, but there were 6 ground truth factors.

> How can the proposed method be used to functionally characterized neurons in the other data modalities, e.g. RNA-seq?

We are not familiar with RNA-seq, though it seems to be for gene sequencing? We are not sure how these methods could be applied there.

> The authors may want to move some of the supplementary materials, e.g. sequential path integration to the main text. It is quit unclear what Eq. 4 is formulating.

Many thanks for the comments. We would like to move much of the appendix to the main text, but we are heavily space limited. Throughout the manuscript, we point to relevant sections in the appendix that go into more detail on sections in the main text. For example, in the paragraph below equation 4, we point to Appendix A.9 that explains the losses in equation 4.

> The paper is overall well organized and well written. Section 4, the rodent navigation task, and the problem definition need some revisions and more clarifications, including Eq. 4, Figure 6 and 7.

We hope that our edits to section 4 (as detailed above) have helped here! We have changed both Figure 6 and 7 as well as the navigation task section (please see paper).

> The paper is addressing a challenging and important problem. The introduced neurobiological perspective and neural representation modeling are novel and interesting.

Many thanks!

> I cannot comment on reproducibility. The code is not available.

We have now included the code as Supplementary Material in this submission.

> I think this is a good submission and the proposed neural representation learning using biological constraints is persuasive. However, I think the authors need to improve section 4 and discuss how these findings are generalizable to the other datasets.

We hope that our improvements to section 4, as well as our extended literature review and clarification that the primary role of this paper is explaining neuroscience results alleviates the reviewer’s concerns.

content.title: Response (1/2)
content.comment:
Many thanks for your thorough read of this paper and extremely helpful comments. The paper is much better for them!

> Although the paper has attempted to make a bridge between neuroscientific findings and the representation learning field, I think the proposed objective is not well-connected to the other studies in this field, except for beta-VAE. It is not clear how the proposed neurobiological constraints improves the already disentangled representations provided by other approaches like factor VAE, weak supervision method (Locatello, ICML, ICLR 2020), or satisfying local isometry (Horan, NeurIPS 2021 ), all of which do not necessarily rely on decorrelation. It is not clear how these neurobiological constraints will complete those approaches. I think the authors need to elaborate more on this.

Many thanks for the comment. We have now expanded the literature review (now in Appendix A.2) that hopefully addresses these concerns. More broadly, however, this paper is primarily a neuroscience paper, and so while we have shown the biological constraints to be useful for disentangling, we are not trying to be state-of-the-art nor are we trying to say that they are better or worse than other models - only that biological constraints do lead to disentangling. We understand this is frustrating for the ML community side who would want to see detailed comparisons to other ML methods. We will address this in future work.

> IID Assumptions: I understand that making iid assumption for the latent (task) factors makes the theoretical justification easier, but in practice, especially in the case of neurons, it is not correct to assume that all neurons follow the same distribution.

Many thanks. We appreciate this comment, and agree that neurons are generally not iid. We made the assumption, as you said, to each theoretical justification. We have added in a sentence (in a footnote) clarifying this.

*We understand that task factors, or indeed neurons in the brain, are generally not i.i.d., but we have made this assumption for mathematical convenience.*

> Domain knowledge: one of the difficulties of learning a disentangled representation is the absence of domain-specific knowledge, like the number of independent factors. According to the problem definition in Eq. 1, to obtain disentangled factors, the network requires access to the true number of K, as I have understood. If this is correct, is there any way to utilize the proposed approach to learn the true number of latent factors?

Many thanks. The theorem applies to an arbitrary representation, where it is not necessary to know the number of factors. In the subsequent sections, none of the networks know a priori the number of factors or any domain knowledge. To disentangle all factors, however, it is necessary that the number of neurons in that layer has more neurons than the number of factors. We have added in a sentence clarifying this.

*No domain knowledge, like the exact number of factors, is provided. However the dimensionality of the network layer must be at least this number to disentangle all factors.*

> The rodent navigation task is a very interesting experimental study. However, the problem formulation in Eq. 4 is quite unclear and confusing.

We apologise for the confusing description. We have now rewritten this section and have also included further details in appendix A.9. The relevant main text addition is shown below:

*Formally, our task requires predicting spatial location, x, whether an object is observed, o, and the optimal action, a. If objects move between tasks, then p(x, a, o) = p(x)p(a, o), where o and a are not factored since optimal actions are dependent on objects (see Appendix A.9 for details). Our theory says the representation will have two subspaces - one for allo- centric location (for predicting x) and one for location relative to objects (for predicting o and a) - and that these sub-spaces should be represented in separate neural populations when biological constraints are present.*

> There experimental results for benchmark datasets are very limited.

We understand your frustration here. As before, this work is primarily for explaining neuroscience results, as opposed to getting state-of-the-art results. The results we have shown are there to convince readers that biological constraints really do achieve disentanglement. Thus we feel that comparisons are not necessary here. We will do so in future work delving into the machine learning side of this work. If the reviewer feels strongly enough, we can try to include further comparisons, but cannot promise it will get done in time.

content.title: Response (6/6)
content.comment:
> Last paragraph section 4: please clarify the distinction and usage of the terms stereotyped behaviour and the concepts of independent factors used so far.

Apologies. In the paper with warped grid cells (Boccara et al., 2019), after the animal finds the 4 rewards, the animal no longer freely explores the environment, but rather sequentially runs between rewards. It does this over and over again, collecting the 4 rewards in sequence using the same spatial trajectories - i.e. a ‘stereotyped behaviour’. We have removed this mention of stereotypes behaviour but made the mention in the previous paragraph clearer with the following sentences:

*Intriguingly, in the warping situation, the rodents exhibited stereotyped behaviour; sequentially running between rewards using the same spatial trajectories rather than freely exploring the space (i.e. behaviour is entangled with space)*

We hope our responses to previous comments (and our newly included text) have made clearer what we mean by independent factors.

> This paper addresses some very interesting questions. They provide an interesting mathematical derivation that could provide a substantial contribution at the intersection of ICA and non-negative factorisation (NMF, sparse coding etc.) literature. However, this would need a much more extensive treatment with more details. I think there are big questions related to the nonlinear setting (see Locatello et al., 2019). The arguments on cell types are interesting. However, the RNN model has a lot of degrees of freedom, the experimental results are unclear and one might wonder if this theory of efficient coding and sources recovery (which needs more links to existing literature) would also apply to, e.g., visual neurons.

We hope that our above responses alleviate your concerns here. We thank you for your enthusiasm on our work though.

> I strongly encourage the authors to split this up into multiple papers and do a more thorough scientific investigation of the different component claims: 1) ICA and non-negativity; 2) non-negativity as inductive bias in nonlinear ICA?; 3) cell types and non-negativity leading to separated components. Each of these questions is very important and interesting and it would be great to give them a proper treatment that creates new scientific insights, ideally with higher SNR than the average ML paper.

This paper will be followed up with both a machine learning paper focusing on non-linear ICA and non-negativity, and a neuroscience paper with data analysis and further explanations of cell types and non-negativity leading to separated components. We do however think that this paper is interesting and worthy of publication in of itself. We hope that we have convinced you of this too!

content.title: Response (5/6)
content.comment:
> Equation 3 needs much more explantation, what is being shown here?

Many thanks for this - it has helped us clarify things. Path integration is usually done through time by an equation like $z_t = f( W_{a} z_{t-1} ) $. If the representation at time-step $ t-1$ corresponds to location $ x - d_a $, then for path integration to be successful, the representation at time $ t $ must correspond to location $ x $. Then the equation becomes like equation 3. This is exactly what our loss asks for (see appendix A.9). It’s true that this is not exactly like path integration since all representations could just be the identity. But when combined with the location loss (see appendix A.9) locations have to be represented differently. These two losses together are then equivalent to path integration. Due to space constraints, we have added in further explanation in appendix A.9 (under ‘structural loss’). We have referenced this in the main text after equation 3. The text in the appendix is:

*This loss is effectively a path integration loss and  can be understood by considering the path integration equation. While there are more than one potential forms for path integration we choose the form relating to Gao et al. 2021 which sequentially updates representations in time via:
$z_t = f( W_{a} z_{t-1} ) $
If the representation at time-step $ t-1$ corresponds to location $ x - d_a $, then for path integration to be successful, the representation at time $ t $ must correspond to location $ x $. Then the equation becomes like equation 3. This is exactly what our loss asks for. We note, however, that this loss on its own could just make all representations at all locations the same constant (and learn all $ W_{a} $ to be the identity), in which case location isn't represented at all. However the location loss ensures all locations are represented differently. So really it is the structural loss and the location loss together that are like path integration. Overall, this formulation translates sequential path integration in time into an optimisation over representation at locations without needing to incorporate time. This greatly reduces the difficulty of optimisation and makes the problem more general than just sequences in time.*

>The sum over loss terms in equation 4 is astonishing, one might wonder whether, with that many degrees of freedom, the model can be forced to produce all sorts of results – put differently, if all these hyperparameters can be adjusted, is it informative if, in the end, a setting is found that leads to the presented results?

The only additional losses, as compared to the earlier ML examples are the three functional losses - these however are required to solve the task - and the structural loss which is required to learn representations that are structured according to space. There isn’t much we can do about that. We agree though that there are lots of moving parts, but still think it is informative being that we have an analytic theory and other simulations that all agree with each other. We do not present a hyperparameter search here because we decided to spend time so far in the rebuttal period responding to other points. We do understand the reviewer’s comments however, and so if the reviewer feels strongly about this, then we will try to do the simulations but cannot promise they will be ready before the paper editing period of rebuttals.

>‘Some cells change a lot, some cells don’t change […] thus, the representation has two disentangled modules’ – what is the quantitative measure for this claim. Honestly, this is frustrating, these are very interesting questions that seem to be dealt with in a hand waivy manner.

Apologies. We have now added a quantitative measure and have shown a double-dissociation between the cells that ‘change a lot’ and the ‘cells that don't’. In particular the cells with representations that do not change between tasks have high grid-score (a measure to determine grid cells) and do not have consistent activity around objects - thus they are grid cells (as can be seen from their rate maps). Whereas cells with representations that change a lot over tasks, have low grid score but instead have consistent firing fields around objects (like object vector cells). These results are now in Figure 6, with a completely reworded caption, and the main text is changed to the following:

*To quantify whether a population really has two distinct cell types (two modules) we analyse the consistency
of a cell’s representation by taking its average spatial correlation between many different object configurations (Fig. 6G-I). In the ReLu case, there are two modes (Fig. 6G-I) showing a double dissociation: the mode containing cells that don’t change have high grid-score (Barry et al., 2012) and do not have consistent activity around objects. These are GCs. Whereas the mode containing cells that change between tasks have low grid-score and respond consistently around objects (Fig. 6H).*

content.title: Response (4/6)
content.comment:
> A factorised task for rodents: second to last sentence, I don’t see how this falls out from the theory?

Many thanks for this - it has made us make things clearer! We have now described the task in terms of variables x, o and a where (space, objects/rewards, and actions respectively). Since the objects/rewards move around between environments p(x,o,a) = p(s)p(o,a) - space and {objects/rewards and actions} are factored, but actions are towards objects/rewards and so are not factoid from each other. Thus if we have a representation that linearly reads out space,  objects/rewards and action, then, from the theory, we expect the space and {object/reward and action} to be represented with different sets of neurons. The new text reads:

*Formally, our task requires predicting spatial location, x, whether an object is observed, o, and the optimal action, a. If objects move between task, then p(x, a, o) = p(x)p(a, o), where o and a are not factored since optimal actions are dependent on objects (see Appendix A.9 for details). Our theory says the representation will have two subspaces - one for allo- centric location (for predicting x) and one for location relative to objects (for predicting o and a) - and that these sub-spaces should be represented in separate neural populations when biological constraints are present.*

> The use of the term path integration is misleading at the beginning of the next paragraph.

We are not sure what the reviewer finds misleading about it. Throughout that paragraph and the following one we have been clear that we have translated the problem of path integrating in a RNN to directly estimating the neural representations of space that afford path-integration. We are happy to make changes, but are unsure what the reviewer has found misleading.

> Fig6: explain the Real OVCS subplot; C) the grids do not appear to be hexagonal or split into modules of different spatial resolution like real GCs? Explain subplots D; explain the spatial correlation and the subplots in H;

We have explained the Real OVC subplot with:

*OVCs encode relative location to objects with firing fields at specific distances and orientations from (white) objects.*

The grid cells are hexagonal. We have now included a grid-score analysis (a measure of being grid cell; Barry et al. 2012) in Figure 6 which shows high scores (above 0.3-0.5 is generally considered a grid cell, and our results show many cells in the range 0.5-1.5). We agree that we only see a single grid module, but the purpose of our work is not to explain every detail of grid cells, but rather explain the distinction between grid cells and object vector cells when tasks are factored.

We have added in an explanation of subplot D with the following text in Figure 6 caption:

*Model ratemaps when trained with a ReLU activation function. Task 1 contains no objects, while task 2 has several objects (white dots). We see two types of cell representation: D) GCs that do not change across tasks and E) OVCs that only appear in the presence of objects.*

 We have explained the spatial correlation subplots with the following text in Figure 6 caption:

*To quantify modules in the ReLu model, we compute the distribution of individual cell spatial correlations across different tasks. H) The mode with high spatial correlation are cells that have high grid-score (Barry et al., 2012) and are grid cells (GCs), the mode with low spatial correlation are cells that respond similarly around objects (OVCs). I) Only one mode of cells is seen without a ReLu activation.*

We have also changed our explanation in the main text (see comment below on ‘Some cells change a lot, some cells don’t change’).
We have changed the explanation of subplot H to

*To quantify module-ness over many random seeds, we compute the cosine distance between the population’s contribution to x and o. This is done by taking the absolute value of weights projecting from z to x and o, then summing over the space/object dimension (to obtain a vector the same dimension as z), then computing the cosine distance. We see low cosine distance for the ReLu indicating different cells code for space vs objects - i.e. modules.*

> 1.1. Reference for Oja rule? Also, there is a whole line of research missing here. Barlow already postulated that neurons perform redundancy reduction, i.e., minimising mutual information between their representations, i.e., finding independent components. BTW, that would also take care of the multiple neurons representing the same factor issue seen here. ‘While it has beeen shown’ +’that’

We have added the reference to Oja’s rule. We have also referred to Barlow, and have stated that while we do not consider parsimony here, that that is also likely an important constraint in biology. Here are the relevant sentences (in the broader literature review - appendix A.2)

*Barlow first hypothesised that neurons represent independent components via redundancy reduction - minimising mutual information between their representation (Barlow, 1961; 1972)*

*We note that Barlow also considered parsimony as a representational pressure too. While we do not consider it in this paper, we believe it is an important constraint.*

> D. in brains: here are other references about disentanglement in brains (https://elifesciences.org/articles/43625.pdf) and (https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/sciadv.aax5979). The second to last sentence needs more explanation.

Many thanks - these are very relevant citations! We have cited both in a broader literature review in appendix A.2 (in appendix due to space constraints).

> 2: what is ‘neural disentangling’? What are a and C? Why is C the same for all neurons? Why minimise the square of the expectation and not the expectation of the square or the variance? Why write |M_jk||M_jl| and not just state that every row of M has exactly one non-zero entry?

We have now included a definition of disentanglement in the introduction, and referred to further details in the appendix A.1.

*We define disentanglement as single neurons responding to single factors of variation (see Appendix A.2 for further details).*

C is the sum of the variance for each neuron, i.e. the population variance, and so is not the same for all neurons. a is the maximum (and - a is the minimum) value that the underlying i.i.d. variables take. Both these points are already stated in Theorem 1 in the main text. We have additionally stated that |M_jk||M_jl| equivalently means that every row of M has exactly one non-zero entry in the following sentence

*$ | M_{jk}| | M_{jl} | = 0 $ for for $ k \neq l$, a.k.a. each row of M has at most 1 non-zero entry.*

> What is the dimensionality of x?

Apologies that this is not stated in the main text. We have changed this now.

> Theorem 2: the zero error assumption seems rather unrealistic?

We agree that it is unrealistic, but for the purposes of this paper we think it is OK. Our future work will include relaxing this assumption.

> Fig 2: What is the scale of the MI matrices? The whole plot and scripts are too small; Define MIR; What is the noise ceiling in D?

The scale of the first MI matrix ranges from 0 to 0.6, the second goes from 0-2.25 (we now mention this in the figure caption). We have increased the size of the plots and text within plots. We now reference the MIR definition in Figure 2 caption. Since we did not add any additional noise to the sampled factors, the noise ceiling is 1. This further highlights the fact that our metric is not the best of all possible metrics, since it is normalised by the mutual information of all factors, rather than just the gap between the factors with 1st and 2nd highest MI, thus it appears lower even with near perfect disentanglement - as can be seen from the MI matrices. Again, we are not trying to introduce a new gold-standard metric, so we feel this is OK and very much still good enough for the central point of this paper. We have added in a paragraph however to state reasons why our metric is not ideal.

*We do not propose this metric as a gold-standard metric for disentanglement, indeed in some situations such as spiral shaped functions, it could exhibit pathological properties. Furthermore since our metric is normalised by the sum mutual information of all factors, rather than the just the gap between factors with 1st and 2nd highest MI, it appears lower even when with near perfect disentanglement.  However in our situations it works just fine. We use it over other metrics since other metrics penalise situations where more than one neuron codes for a ground-truth factor.*

> The authors claim their results provide a potential explanation for concept cells (i.e. grandmother cells) but if energy considerations favor disentangled codes, we would expect to find selective codes for every single concept. Clearly, allowing specialized cells for all concepts in complex domains would be impossible as we’d run out of neural hardware. It would be useful if the authors could discuss the trade-offs or speculate about how such trade-offs might be handled by the brain.

Thanks for the comment! To decode N concepts linearly, then you need at least N neurons to do so. All we are saying is that each of those N neurons will favour coding for just one concept, rather than a mixture. It is true that with non-linear decoding you can get away with fewer neurons, but at some point you’ll have to decode into N neurons anyway - and if using neural networks that requires at least N neurons. Our belief is that we don’t require a linear readout of every concept, i.e. some concepts are implicit and not explicitly read out, thus you don’t need a neuron for every concept. We now include the following sentence. 

*We note that while our theory says you need at least one neuron per concept that is read-out (true even without disentanglement), it does not say you need a neuron for every possible concept - only for ones that are explicitly read-out.*

> I understand that space might be a limiting factor but it would be helpful to situate their work within the context of a broader literature on disentangling in machines (besides beta-VAE). There is plenty evidence of disentangling in machines as an emergent phenomenon (not baked in) for e.g. the work of David Bau et al. who found interpretable neurons in vision models, multimodal neurons in CLIP (https://distill.pub/2021/multimodal-neurons/), other work by on superposition/ privileged axes (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html) that also discusses the role of non-negativity constraints etc. There is also other work on understanding specialization in DNNs that could be relevant: https://openreview.net/forum?id=HreeeJvkue9.

Many thanks for the comment and pointing us to those works. We have included these works in a broader literature review in appendix A.2 (due to space constraints).

> I found this work to be of very high-quality and consider this to be a novel and original contribution to the field.

Many thanks!

> I think the paper is exceptionally written and conveys the ideas very well.
The paper is a nice mix of theory and experiments along with a biological case simulation. The authors also present an intuition accompanying the theorem which nicely illustrates the logic.
Instead of simply comparing representations at the population level which has been the dominant approach in neuroAI, the paper compares representations at the level of axes, i.e. why the brain and ANNs often develop privileged axes. This is an intriguing question that has received little attention in the field so far and I laud the authors for tackling this with clarity.

Many thanks!

> I think the justification behind non-negativity (of firing rates) as a biological constraint needs some further discussion in the paper. It is known that the firing activity of single neurons can be suppressed (from baseline rates) and activity is always going to be measured with respect to some reference signal/rate.

Many thanks for the comment - it has helped us clarify the paper. We agree that firing below baseline can be viewed as ‘negative’ firing - in fact this is exactly how our proof works! Activity below baseline corresponds to negative/positive values in the distribution, and activity above baseline corresponds to positive/negative values in the distribution. We only require that firing below baseline does not go below zero activity. We have clarified this in the paper with:

*We note that this is consistent with neurons having a baseline firing rate where now activity below baseline corresponds to negative/positive values in the distribution, and activity above baseline corresponds to positive/negative values in the distribution.*

> The constraints the authors frame as ‘biological constraints’ are both routinely employed in modern CNNs through ReLU and l1 regularization on activity/weights. In that context, I found the use of the phrase ‘biological constraints’ to be a bit overblown.

Many thanks for the comment. We don’t claim that these constraints are anything new to the community as they, or similar, have been used many times in the literature. However, putting them under the umbrella of biological constraints and then understanding the impact that biology then has on representations is new. We clarify this in the paper.

*While these constraints of nonnegativity and energy efficiency are not new to the machine learning or neuroscience literature, we package them together to learn new insights into how biological constraints shape the space of neural representation.*

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper asks the question of why neural systems often develop a factorized or disentangled representation, i.e. a representation which aligns its variables/latent units with a meaningful factorization of the underlying problem structure. The authors use a combination of theory and simulations to show that biological constraints of non-negative and energy-efficiency together gives rise to disentangled representations. Finally taking the specialized cells in hippocampus like grid cells and object vector cells as a biological case in point, the authors simulate spatial processing in ANNs and demonstrate that biological constraints lead to disentangled codes for space and objects when these factors are independent, but the same constraints lead to entangled codes when these factors do not vary independently in a task, providing a potential explanation (specifically) for why grid cells warp their receptive fields and (more generally) for when and why disentangled codes arise in the brain.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- I think the paper is exceptionally written and conveys the ideas very well. 
- The paper is a nice mix of theory and experiments along with a biological case simulation. The authors also present an intuition accompanying the theorem which nicely illustrates the logic.
- Instead of simply comparing representations at the population level which has been the dominant approach in neuroAI, the paper compares representations at the level of axes, i.e. why the brain and ANNs often develop privileged axes. This is an intriguing question that has received little attention in the field so far and I laud the authors for tackling this with clarity. 

Weaknesses: 
- I think the justification behind non-negativity (of firing rates) as a biological constraint needs some further discussion in the paper. It is known that the firing activity of single neurons can be suppressed (from baseline rates) and activity is always going to be measured with respect to some reference signal/rate. The constraints the authors frame as ‘biological constraints’ are both routinely employed in modern CNNs through ReLU and l1 regularization on activity/weights. In that context, I found the use of the phrase ‘biological constraints’ to be a bit overblown. 
- The authors claim their results provide a potential explanation for concept cells (i.e. grandmother cells) but if energy considerations favor disentangled codes, we would expect to find selective codes for every single concept. Clearly, allowing specialized cells for all concepts in complex domains would be impossible as we’d run out of neural hardware. It would be useful if the authors could discuss the trade-offs or speculate about how such trade-offs might be handled by the brain. 
- I understand that space might be a limiting factor but it would be helpful to situate their work within the context of a broader literature on disentangling in machines (besides beta-VAE). There is plenty evidence of disentangling in machines as an emergent phenomenon (not baked in) for e.g. the work of David Bau et al. who found interpretable neurons in vision models, multimodal neurons in CLIP (https://distill.pub/2021/multimodal-neurons/), other work by on superposition/ privileged axes (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html) that also discusses the role of non-negativity constraints etc. There is also other work on understanding specialization in DNNs that could be relevant: https://openreview.net/forum?id=HreeeJvkue9.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The manuscript introduced a bio-inspired representation learning that guarantees disentanglement in linear network, under some assumptions. The authors showed two neurobiological constraints i.e., nonnegativity and minimum energy efficiency (with respect to activity and weights), lead to linear factorization, under iid assumption of true factors. Additionally, the authors utilized the proposed biological constraints to interpret cell types which are functionally distinct. The authors used multiple simulated scenarios to demonstrate the performance of the proposed approach for linear and non-linear networks, under supervised and unsupervised fashion. Additionally, they reported their model disentanglement performance in comparison with beta-VAE for a few examples of benchmark datasets including Shape3D, dSprites and a rodent navigation task.

**Update after rebuttal:** I have read the author's rebuttal and the latest revision. The authors have satisfactorily addressed most of questions/concerns and improved the manuscript by providing more details and clarification. After reading the rebuttal and the response to the other reviewers, I'm happy to raise my score to help the paper getting accepted.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 

- The paper is addressing a challenging and important problem, learning disentangled and interpretable latent factors, from a neurobiological perspective, which in my opinion is quite interesting and novel. The authors provide a simple set of constraints which lead to a disentangled representation which are quite valuable and potentially could expand the findings of the previous disentanglement studies.

- The main claim of the manuscript is theoretically and empirically justified. 

- The simulation studies illustrate that under iid the proposed metric reveal the disentanglement decrement under entanglement attacks, while the comparable measures fail to present it.

- The authors provide multiple experimental settings to evalute the proposed method. 


Limitations: 

- Although the paper has attempted to make a bridge between neuroscientific findings and the representation learning field, I think the proposed objective is not well-connected to the other studies in this field, except for beta-VAE. It is not clear how the proposed neurobiological constraints improves the already disentangled representations provided by other approaches like factor VAE, weak supervision method (Locatello, ICML, ICLR 2020), or satisfying local isometry (Horan, NeurIPS 2021 ), all of which do not necessarily rely on decorrelation. It is not clear how these neurobiological constraints will complete those approaches. I think the authors need to elaborate more on this.

- IID Assumptions: I understand that making iid assumption for the latent (task) factors makes the theoretical justification easier, but in practice, especially in the case of neurons, it is not correct to assume that all neurons follow the same distribution.

- Domain knowledge: one of the difficulties of learning a disentangled representation is the absence of domain-specific knowledge, like the number of independent factors. According to the problem definition in Eq. 1, to obtain disentangled factors, the network requires access to the true number of K, as I have understood. If this is correct, is there any way to utilize the proposed approach to learn the true number of latent factors?

- The rodent navigation task is a very interesting experimental study. However, the problem formulation in Eq. 4 is quite unclear and confusing. 

- There experimental results for benchmark datasets are very limited.

Additional Comment/Questions:

- Is the rodent navigation dataset a new dataset used in this paper? What are the modalities of the given data (measurements)? 
- Can you elaborate more on your findings in Figure 7? How should one compare the results in Figures 6 and 7?

- How would this model perform when K is not matched with the true number of factors? In the case of cell type, how can one interpret the results in terms of the function of each neuron?

- How can the proposed method be used to functionally characterized neurons in the other data modalities, e.g. RNA-seq? 

- The authors may want to move some of the supplementary materials, e.g. sequential path integration to the main text. It is quit unclear what Eq. 4 is formulating.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: 

The paper is overall well organized and well written.
Section 4, the rodent navigation task, and the problem definition need some revisions and more clarifications, including Eq. 4, Figure 6 and 7.


Quality: 

The paper is technical with enough theoretical backing. Theorem 1 shows that in the presence of iid latent factors and nonnegativity of neural activities with constant variance, the representations that achieve minimal activity energy also exhibit disentangling. Theorem 2 generalizes the result of the first theorem by considering generative model for neural representations that can exactly predict the observed data, without requiring constant variance.

Novelty and Originality:

The paper is addressing a challenging and important problem. The introduced neurobiological perspective and neural representation modeling are novel and interesting. 

Reproducibility:

I cannot comment on reproducibility. The code is not available.

content.title: Disentanglement with Biological Constraints: A Theory of Functional Cell Types
content.abstract: Neurons in the brain are often finely tuned for specific task variables. Moreover, such disentangled representations are highly sought after in machine learning. Here we mathematically prove that simple biological constraints on neurons, namely nonnegativity and energy efficiency in both activity and weights, promote such sought after disentangled representations by enforcing neurons to become selective for single factors of task variation. We demonstrate these constraints lead to disentanglement in a variety of tasks and architectures, including variational autoencoders. We also use this theory to explain why the brain partitions its cells into distinct cell types such as grid and object-vector cells, and also explain when the brain instead entangles representations in response to entangled task factors. Overall, this work provides a mathematical understanding of why single neurons in the brain often represent single human-interpretable factors, and steps towards an understanding task structure shapes the structure of brain representation.
